newsitem.title: south africa: Tutu says cancer spreads, needs more treatment.
newsitem.headline: Tutu says cancer spreads, needs more treatment.

text.p: South African Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu said on Wednesday his prostate cancer appeared to have spread and he would go to the United States for radiation therapy.
But when he spoke to reporters after meeting Hillary Rodham Clinton, wife of the US president, Tutu, 65, was as cheerful as always and said: "I'm feeling good."
Tutu, a leading campaigner in the fight against apartheid, had most of his prostate cut out in January when the gland was diagnosed as cancerous.
Doctors told him at the time he would need further surgery or treatment with radiation and hormones.

Tutu, now head of South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission probing apartheid crimes, said in a statement that after consulting doctors in the United States last week he had decided on a combination of hormone treatment and radiotherapy.
"I have been advised that the cancer is suspected to have penetrated beyond the prostate gland and that as a result radiotherapy is the best option," he said.

"Medical specialists in Cape Town will begin a three-month course of hormone treatment tomorrow (Thursday) ... After the hormone treatment, I plan to have the radiotherapy at a clinic in the United States. This will take two months."
Asked later how bad the prognosis was, Tutu said there were indications, but no absolute certainty, that the cancer had taken a critical turn.
"If it has, then it has," he said.

He said doctors at two U.S. clinics, Johns Hopkins Medical Centre in Baltimore and the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Centre in New York, had told him radiation therapy was "as good an option as any."

He said that while he was in the United States he would set up an office through which he would keep close touch with the truth commission, which is investigating human rights abuses by both sides of the apartheid divide.
"I hope I won't be too decrepit by then," he joked.
Tutu, lauded as the conscience of South Africa, was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1984 for his efforts to end apartheid.
But he has not hesitated to criticise President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, which won historic elections in April 1994, over what he sees as its weaknesses or failings.
He said on Wednesday he hoped to follow a normal schedule during the hormone treatment in Cape Town ... "but will be unable to continue squeezing additional commitments in the schedule".
He told Clinton he had the support of excellent staff and colleagues and that his absence from the commission, which ends its work in December, would not be significant. FER PH
